title: Along the Rhine
hook: Jewish communities grow in German and French towns along the Rhine

segments.voice: Yesterday, Italy and Byzantium, and the communities that stayed. Your line was old communities. Today we follow a road north.

A river barge drifts down the Rhine, past vineyards and the towers of cathedral towns. On board are bolts of cloth, barrels of wine, and a few merchants who stop work every Friday before dark. Where the boat ties up, in towns like Speyer, Worms and Mainz, small Jewish quarters have taken root: a synagogue, a ritual bath, a study house, a cemetery at the edge of town. Families who will one day be called Ashkenazi Jews are starting out here. And their name wasn't invented on the Rhine. It comes from a single line in Genesis.
screen: `A BARGE ON THE RHINE.` → `SPEYER, WORMS, MAINZ.` → `A NAME FROM GENESIS.`

segments.voice: Open Genesis chapter ten, the long list of nations after the flood. Among the grandsons of Japheth, the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation lists the sons of Gomer: "Ashkenaz, and Riphath, and Togarmah." Just one name in a family tree, no story attached. But medieval Jews read those lists as a map of the world, and gave the old biblical names to the lands around them. Ashkenaz came to mean the German lands, and the Jews there became Ashkenazim. A name from the edge of a genealogy became the name of a whole branch of the Jewish people. Now the towns. Speyer, Worms and Mainz each had a Hebrew name, and the first letters of those names were put together into one word: Shum. The three communities worked so closely that people spoke of them as a single unit. Their leaders met, their scholars taught each other's students, and their rulings traveled along the river. Where did the learning come from? Tradition says a scholarly family from Lucca in Italy was brought north to Mainz, and their descendants became teachers and poets there: yesterday's thread, over the Alps. These were small places. A merchant community in a Christian town lived by charters, permissions from a local bishop or ruler that could be granted and taken away. Life could be good, and then suddenly it was not. We'll come back to the dangers. For now, hold the first picture: a study house on a river bank, students copying, families keeping the Sabbath through a cold northern winter.
screen: `ASHKENAZ: A NAME IN GENESIS.` · then, large: `ASHKENAZ, AND RIPHATH, AND TOGARMAH.` · `SHUM: SPEYER, WORMS, MAINZ.` · `LEARNING CARRIED NORTH FROM ITALY.`

segments.voice: Go back as far as you know of your family: a grandparent's town, a great-grandparent's country; if you don't know, notice that too, gently. Was there a river, a road or a port that carried them, and what did they bring that you still have, a word, a dish, a name? If you pray, you can remember them in words from your own tradition.
Ashkenaz. A name from the family tree in Genesis that medieval Jews gave to the German lands, and so to the Jews who lived there. Today's word.
Your line: the rhine communities. Small towns, and learning that traveled the river. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ashkenazi Jews trace their customs and prayer rite to the medieval communities of the German and French lands, and the old Jewish sites of Speyer, Worms and Mainz are visited and remembered today.
